title: Grade 5 Science — Thu, Jun 12
description: The Digestive System — Day 4 of 5: Nutrition labels, timeline, and digestive problems
subject: science

questions.question: Approximately how long does it take for food to pass completely through the digestive system?
options: 6–8 hours in small intestine + 24–72 hours total
questions.explanation: Food spends about 4–5 hours in the stomach, 6–8 hours in the small intestine, and 12–48 hours in the large intestine.

questions.question: Food stays the longest in which part of the digestive system?
questions.explanation: The large intestine is where waste stays the longest (up to 48 hours) while water is slowly absorbed.

questions.question: A nutrition label on a food packet tells you:
options: The amounts of nutrients (calories, protein, fat, carbs, etc.) in a serving
questions.explanation: Nutrition labels show serving size and the amounts of energy, macronutrients, vitamins, and minerals per serving.

questions.question: On a nutrition label, 'Calories' (or kJ) represents:
options: Amount of energy the body gets from the food
questions.explanation: Calories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ) measure how much energy a food provides to the body.

questions.question: Constipation is caused by:
options: Too little water and fibre, causing hard stools that are difficult to pass
questions.explanation: Constipation occurs when waste moves too slowly through the large intestine. Lack of fibre and water are common causes.

questions.question: Diarrhoea is when:
options: Watery stools are passed frequently because the large intestine cannot absorb water normally
The stomach makes too much acid
questions.explanation: Diarrhoea is caused by infections or irritants that speed up food movement, preventing the large intestine from absorbing water.

questions.question: Eating too fast and swallowing air often causes:
questions.explanation: Eating quickly means less chewing and more swallowed air, leading to indigestion, bloating, or burping.

questions.question: Acidity (heartburn) is caused by:
options: Stomach acid flowing back up into the oesophagus
questions.explanation: Acidity occurs when gastric acid flows back (reflux) into the oesophagus, causing a burning sensation in the chest.

questions.question: Eating fibre-rich food like whole grains and vegetables helps prevent:
questions.explanation: Dietary fibre adds bulk to stools and helps food move smoothly through the intestines, preventing constipation.

questions.question: Food poisoning is caused by eating food contaminated with:
questions.explanation: Bacterial contamination (e.g., Salmonella, E. coli) in food causes food poisoning — symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea.

questions.question: Which practice helps prevent digestive problems?
options: Chewing food well and eating slowly
Drinking cold drinks with every meal
questions.explanation: Chewing thoroughly breaks food into smaller pieces, mixes it well with saliva, and makes digestion easier.

questions.question: Drinking clean, boiled water helps prevent:
options: Water-borne diseases like cholera and typhoid
questions.explanation: Many infections (cholera, typhoid, dysentery) spread through contaminated water. Boiling or filtering water kills pathogens.

questions.question: Reading a nutrition label, you see '15g of sugar per serving'. This is the amount of:
questions.explanation: Sugar on a nutrition label is a type of carbohydrate. 15g per serving means 15g of sugar that provides energy.

questions.question: The recommended daily calorie intake for a 10-year-old child is approximately:
questions.explanation: Children aged 9–13 need about 1,600–2,200 kcal per day, depending on their activity level.

questions.question: Which of the following is a healthy habit for good digestion?
options: Eating at regular times, staying hydrated, and including fibre
questions.explanation: Regular meal timings, adequate water, and fibre-rich foods support healthy digestion and prevent most digestive problems.
